questions.subject: THERMODYNAMICS
questions.learningObjective: Apply Boltzmann Population Ratio principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: In a calibration run, two brass energy levels are separated by 4.21e-21 J. At 331 K compute the Boltzmann population ratio of the upper to the lower level.

options.misconception: Reported the exponent itself rather than its exponential
Inserted an extra factor of two in the denominator
Correct application of the principle
Used a positive exponent and exceeded one

questions.explanation: The Boltzmann distribution gives the upper-to-lower population ratio as exp of minus delta E over kT. With separation 4.2e-21 J, k equal to 1.380649e-23, and 331 K the ratio is 0.3981; since the upper level lies higher, fewer molecules occupy it at thermal equilibrium.
questions.hint: N_upper/N_lower = exp(-delta E / kT).

options.misconception: Used three kT instead of three halves kT
Used the gas constant instead of the Boltzmann constant
Correct application of the principle
Omitted the three translational degrees of freedom

questions.explanation: Each translational degree of freedom contributes half of kT, and there are three, so the mean translational kinetic energy is three halves kT. With 594 K and k equal to 1.380649e-23 the result is 1.23e-20 J; note this is per molecule, which is why Boltzmann's constant rather than R appears.
questions.hint: Average translational KE = (3/2) kT per molecule.

questions.subject: THERMODYNAMICS
questions.learningObjective: Apply van der Waals Pressure principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: In a laboratory check, for 1.6 mol of krypton in 10.6 L at 348 K, use the van der Waals equation with a 4.40 and b 0.097 and R 0.08314 L bar per mol K to find the pressure in bar.

options.misconception: Correct application of the principle
Used the ideal gas law and ignored both corrections
Applied only the excluded-volume attraction and omitted the b correction
Applied only the volume correction and omitted the attraction term

questions.explanation: The van der Waals equation corrects the ideal law for molecular attraction and finite size: P equals nRT over (V minus nb) minus a n squared over V squared. With the given constants and 1.6 mol at 348 K, the pressure is 4.33 bar; the attraction lowers pressure while excluded volume raises it.
questions.hint: P = nRT/(V - nb) - a(n/V)^2 using van der Waals constants.

questions.stem: In a benchtop measurement, a nitrogen sample has pressure 20 atm, volume 2.23 L, 1.2 mol, and temperature 392 K. Compute its compressibility factor Z using R 0.082057.

options.misconception: Inverted the compressibility-factor ratio
Correct application of the principle
Used the energy-based gas constant in a L atm expression
Shifted the temperature before computing Z

questions.explanation: The compressibility factor is Z equals PV over nRT, measuring deviation from ideality; Z equals one for an ideal gas. With pressure 20 atm, volume 2.23 L, 1.2 mol, and 392 K the value is 1.155; values below one indicate net attractive interactions.
questions.hint: Z = PV/(nRT) with R consistent with the pressure and volume units.

questions.stem: In a practice exercise, for a helium gas modelled with van der Waals constants a 3.25 and b 0.053, molar heat capacity 48 J per mol K, and temperature 440 K, estimate the Joule-Thomson coefficient in K per bar using R 0.08314.

options.misconception: Correct application of the principle
Omitted the heat-capacity divisor
Reversed the sign of the coefficient
Used only half the attraction term

questions.explanation: For a van der Waals gas the Joule-Thomson coefficient is approximately (1/Cp) times (2a over RT minus b). Substituting a 3.25, b 0.053, Cp 48, and 440 K gives 0.0026 K per bar; a positive value means throttling cools the gas, which is exploited in liquefaction.
questions.hint: Mu_JT ~ (1/Cp)(2a/(RT) - b) for a van der Waals gas.

Used a negative sign before the virial term

questions.learningObjective: Apply Fugacity principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: In a skills drill, a krypton gas at 27 bar has a fugacity coefficient of 1.119; compute its fugacity in bar.

options.misconception: Correct application of the principle
Used one minus the coefficient times pressure
Added the coefficient to the pressure
Divided pressure by the fugacity coefficient

questions.explanation: Fugacity is the effective pressure that replaces pressure in thermodynamic expressions for real gases, defined as the fugacity coefficient times the true pressure, f equals phi P. With coefficient 1.119 and pressure 27 bar the fugacity is 30.21 bar; an ideal gas has phi equal to one so f equals P.
questions.hint: Fugacity f = phi P, where phi is the fugacity coefficient.
